_comment: Per-author extras for the Library and 'Did you know?'. set = one of poets|novelists|playwrights|thinkers|scientists|leaders|essayists. fact = one short, true, kid-safe sentence. Editorially reviewed.

William Shakespeare.fact: His plays were performed at the Globe, a round wooden theatre beside the River Thames in London.

Alexander Pope.fact: At his riverside villa in Twickenham he built a famous grotto decorated with shells, minerals and mirrors.

John Milton.fact: Milton knew many languages and worked as a government secretary writing official letters in Latin.

Lord Byron.fact: As a student at Cambridge he kept a tame bear, because the college rules did not forbid bears.

William Wordsworth.fact: He loved long walks and often composed his poems aloud while strolling the hills of the Lake District.

Plutarch.fact: Shakespeare used an English translation of his work as a source for plays such as Julius Caesar.

Samuel Johnson.fact: Johnson had a cat named Hodge and would go out himself to buy oysters for it.

Alfred, Lord Tennyson.fact: His voice was recorded on an Edison wax cylinder in 1890, reading one of his own poems aloud.

Oliver Goldsmith.fact: His comedy She Stoops to Conquer first opened in 1773 and is still performed on stages today.

William Cowper.fact: Cowper kept three pet hares named Puss, Tiney and Bess, and wrote about them for a magazine.

Miguel de Cervantes.fact: Don Quixote is often called the first modern novel, and its hero famously fights windmills he thinks are giants.

Marcus Aurelius.fact: A bronze statue of him riding a horse has survived in Rome since ancient times and is now in a museum.

James Russell Lowell.fact: Lowell was the first editor of The Atlantic Monthly, the magazine that began in Boston in 1857.

John Dryden.fact: Dryden spent so much time at Will's Coffee House in London that he had his own chair by the fire.

Thomas Moore.fact: He was a close friend of Lord Byron and later published a famous book of Byron's letters and life.

Robert Burton.fact: He published his famous book under the playful pen name Democritus Junior, after a laughing Greek thinker.

Samuel Butler.fact: King Charles II enjoyed his comic poem so much that he often quoted lines from it.

Edward Young.fact: Night Thoughts was so popular that the artist William Blake painted hundreds of watercolours for it.

Ralph Waldo Emerson.fact: Emerson let his friend Henry David Thoreau build a small cabin on his land beside Walden Pond.

Robert Burns.fact: Every 25 January, people around the world hold Burns Night suppers with haggis to celebrate his birthday.

Samuel Taylor Coleridge.fact: He and Wordsworth published Lyrical Ballads together in 1798, a book that helped start English Romanticism.

Sir Walter Scott.fact: He published his novels without his name at first, which earned him the nickname "The Great Unknown".

Robert Browning.fact: His poem The Pied Piper of Hamelin, about a piper who leads away the rats of a town, is a children's favourite.

Michel de Montaigne.fact: Latin was his first language: his father had everyone in the house speak only Latin to him as a child.

Henry Wadsworth Longfellow.fact: He was the first American writer honoured with a bust in Poets' Corner at Westminster Abbey.

Geoffrey Chaucer.fact: Chaucer wrote a guide to the astrolabe, an instrument for measuring the stars, for a boy named Lewis.

Francis Bacon.fact: He championed learning by experiment and observation, an idea that shaped the modern scientific method.

Jonathan Swift.fact: The tiny people of Lilliput in his book gave English the word "Lilliputian", meaning very small.

Richard Brinsley Sheridan.fact: His character Mrs Malaprop, who keeps mixing up her words, gave English the word "malapropism".

Thomas Campbell.fact: He was one of the leading founders of the University of London, now known as University College London.

Edmund Burke.fact: He was one of the first members of The Club, a London dining group started by Joshua Reynolds and Samuel Johnson.

Benjamin Disraeli.fact: He published his first novel, Vivian Grey, in 1826, when he was only about 21 years old.

Thomas Gray.fact: Afraid of fire, he had an iron bar fitted at his Cambridge window to hold a rope ladder for escape.

François de La Rochefoucauld.fact: His book of Maxims holds hundreds of short sayings, which he polished and revised over many years.

Epictetus.fact: Epictetus wrote nothing down himself; his student Arrian recorded his lessons for later readers.

James Thomson.fact: He wrote the words of Rule, Britannia!, the famous song set to music by the composer Thomas Arne.

François Rabelais.fact: Before writing his comic tales, he trained and worked as a doctor in the French city of Lyon.

Thomas Hood.fact: For years he wrote and illustrated his own Comic Annual, packed with puns and funny drawings.

Edmund Spenser.fact: Spenser invented the Spenserian stanza, a nine-line verse form later used by Keats, Byron and Shelley.

Sydney Smith.fact: He gave popular lectures on moral philosophy at the Royal Institution in London that drew big crowds.

Oliver Wendell Holmes Sr..fact: His poem Old Ironsides helped save the famous warship USS Constitution from being scrapped.

Percy Bysshe Shelley.fact: His wife, Mary Shelley, wrote the famous novel Frankenstein, first published in 1818.

George Chapman.fact: Keats wrote a famous sonnet, On First Looking into Chapman's Homer, praising his translation.

John Gay.fact: The Beggar's Opera was the model for The Threepenny Opera, written by Bertolt Brecht two centuries later.

George Herbert.fact: Some of his poems are printed in special shapes, such as Easter Wings, which looks like a pair of wings.

Benjamin Franklin.fact: Franklin invented bifocal glasses, the lightning rod and a stove that heated rooms more safely.

Thomas Percy.fact: His collection of old ballads thrilled the young Walter Scott and helped inspire the Romantic poets.

Thomas Babington Macaulay.fact: A famous reader, he could memorise long poems after one reading and recite them years later.

John Lyly.fact: The fancy, pattern-filled style of his Euphues gave English the word "euphuism" for showy writing.

Izaak Walton.fact: The Compleat Angler has been reprinted hundreds of times, making it one of the most reprinted books in English.

James Montgomery.fact: His hymn Angels from the Realms of Glory is still sung at Christmas in many countries.

Daniel Webster.fact: He was the lawyer who won the famous Dartmouth College case before the US Supreme Court in 1819.

John Keats.fact: Before becoming a full-time poet, Keats trained as an apothecary and studied at Guy's Hospital in London.

Abraham Cowley.fact: He published his first book of poems, Poetical Blossoms, when he was just 15 years old.

Matthew Prior.fact: As a boy he was found reading the Latin poet Horace by an earl, who then helped pay for his schooling.

Joseph Addison.fact: He created Sir Roger de Coverley, a kindly country gentleman, as a much-loved character in The Spectator.

Isaac Watts.fact: His poem about the little busy bee was later playfully parodied by Lewis Carroll in Alice in Wonderland.

Thomas Carlyle.fact: When the only manuscript of his history of the French Revolution was accidentally burned, he rewrote it all.

Thomas Middleton.fact: His play A Game at Chess, with characters as chess pieces, drew huge crowds in London in 1624.

Thomas Haynes Bayly.fact: His song Long, Long Ago became one of the most popular parlour songs of the 1800s.

Thomas Fuller.fact: His book The Worthies of England is full of lively facts about famous people from each county.

Ben Jonson.fact: In 1618 he walked all the way from London to Edinburgh, a journey of roughly 400 miles.

Robert Herrick.fact: Before going to university, he spent several years training as a goldsmith under his uncle in London.

Sir Walter Raleigh.fact: The city of Raleigh, the capital of North Carolina, is named after him.

Edmund Waller.fact: Dryden and other later poets praised him for making English rhyming verse sound smoother.

Samuel Rogers.fact: A wealthy banker, he hosted famous breakfasts in London for the leading writers and artists of his day.

Felicia Hemans.fact: Her first book of poems was published in 1808, when she was only about 14 years old.

Douglas Jerrold.fact: He was one of the early star writers for Punch, the famous British comic magazine.

Elizabeth Barrett Browning.fact: Her pet spaniel Flush was so famous that Virginia Woolf later wrote a whole book about him.

John Selden.fact: He owned a huge collection of books and manuscripts, many of which went to Oxford's Bodleian Library.

Sir Thomas Browne.fact: He is credited with bringing the word "electricity" into English, in a 1646 book about common mistakes.

George Crabbe.fact: Benjamin Britten's opera Peter Grimes is based on a story from his long poem The Borough.

Charles Lamb.fact: With his sister Mary he wrote Tales from Shakespeare, retelling the plays for children.

Christopher Marlowe.fact: The son of a shoemaker in Canterbury, he went to Cambridge University on a scholarship.

Colley Cibber.fact: Alexander Pope made him the king of the dunces in a later version of his comic poem The Dunciad.

Edward Gibbon.fact: He got the idea for his great history while sitting among the ruins of ancient Rome in 1764.

Edward Bulwer-Lytton.fact: A yearly contest for the worst possible opening sentence of a novel is named after him.

Molière.fact: Born Jean-Baptiste Poquelin, the son of a royal upholsterer, he chose a stage name for his acting career.

Blaise Pascal.fact: As a teenager he built one of the first mechanical calculators to help his father with tax sums.

John Fletcher.fact: Fletcher worked with Shakespeare on some of his later plays, including The Two Noble Kinsmen.

Henry Carey.fact: He gave English the word "namby-pamby" as a teasing nickname for the poet Ambrose Philips.

William Congreve.fact: His first comedy, The Old Bachelor, was a big hit in 1693, when he was only about 23.

William Shenstone.fact: His garden at The Leasowes became so famous that visitors travelled from far away to walk in it.

William Collins.fact: His Ode to Evening is unusual because it does not rhyme, yet it is one of his best-loved poems.

Charles Churchill.fact: His first big success, The Rosciad, poked fun at the actors of the London stage.

James Beattie.fact: He wrote a list of "Scotticisms" to help Scottish writers avoid Scottish words in formal English.

Robert Southey.fact: He published the first known printed version of the story The Three Bears, in 1837.

John Greenleaf Whittier.fact: His long poem Snow-Bound describes a family snowed in at their farmhouse during a winter storm.

Tacitus.fact: His short book Germania is one of the earliest written descriptions of the peoples of ancient Germany.

Pliny the Younger.fact: As a teenager he saw Mount Vesuvius erupt in AD 79 and later described it in famous letters.

Sir Philip Sidney.fact: He wrote The Defence of Poesy, one of the first great essays in English on why poetry matters.

Samuel Daniel.fact: He served as tutor to the young Lady Anne Clifford, who later became a famous diarist.

Sir John Suckling.fact: He is often credited with inventing the card game cribbage, which is still played today.

Andrew Marvell.fact: He worked alongside John Milton as an assistant in the government's office for foreign languages.

Lord Chesterfield.fact: He helped Britain switch to the Gregorian calendar in 1752, when 11 days were skipped.

Robert Blair.fact: His son, also named Robert Blair, became one of Scotland's top judges as Lord President.

William Cullen Bryant.fact: He was an early champion of creating a great public park in New York, which became Central Park.

Samuel Lover.fact: Lover wrote Handy Andy, a comic novel about a clumsy but lovable young Irish servant.

Charles Mackay.fact: His book Extraordinary Popular Delusions describes crazes like Tulip Mania, when bulbs sold for fortunes.

Matthew Arnold.fact: For about 35 years he worked as a school inspector, visiting schools all over England.

Jean de La Fontaine.fact: French schoolchildren still learn his fables by heart, such as The Grasshopper and the Ant.

Voltaire.fact: Voltaire was a pen name; his real name was Francois-Marie Arouet, and he was born in Paris.

Sir Henry Wotton.fact: He served as English ambassador to Venice and later became Provost of Eton College.

John Webster.fact: His best-known plays, The Duchess of Malfi and The White Devil, are still staged around the world.

Thomas Dekker.fact: His cheerful comedy The Shoemaker's Holiday is about a London shoemaker who becomes Lord Mayor.

Henry Vaughan.fact: He had a twin brother, Thomas Vaughan, who became a well-known writer on alchemy.

Thomas Tickell.fact: His translation of the first book of the Iliad came out the same week as Pope's, sparking a rivalry.

Lady Mary Wortley Montagu.fact: Her lively letters describe her time in Constantinople, where her husband served as British ambassador.

Edward Moore.fact: He edited The World, a weekly paper with famous contributors such as Lord Chesterfield.

Laurence Sterne.fact: Tristram Shandy includes a completely black page, a marbled page and squiggly lines showing its plot.

David Garrick.fact: Garrick organised the first big Shakespeare festival, the Jubilee at Stratford-upon-Avon, in 1769.

Thomas Jefferson.fact: Jefferson sold his personal library of thousands of books to Congress to help rebuild the Library of Congress.

Leigh Hunt.fact: He helped introduce Keats and Shelley to readers by printing their early poems in his newspaper.

Richard Monckton Milnes.fact: He wrote the first major biography of the poet John Keats, published in 1848.

Edgar Allan Poe.fact: The Baltimore Ravens American football team is named after his poem The Raven.

Richard Lovelace.fact: He belonged to the Cavalier poets, a group of witty writers at the court of King Charles I.

Nicholas Rowe.fact: In 1709 he published one of the first edited collections of Shakespeare's plays, with a short life of him.

Mark Akenside.fact: His long poem The Pleasures of Imagination was a big success when he was only in his early twenties.

Anna Laetitia Barbauld.fact: Her Lessons for Children were among the first books printed in large, easy type for young readers.

Charles Dibdin.fact: Besides writing songs, he composed music, performed one-man shows and ran a small theatre in London.

Hannah More.fact: As a young woman, she helped run a girls' boarding school in Bristol with her sisters.

George Colman the Younger.fact: He managed the Haymarket Theatre in London, which his father had run before him.

George Canning.fact: As a pupil at Eton he helped start a school magazine called The Microcosm.

Henry Clay.fact: Clay was nicknamed "The Great Compromiser" for helping settle bitter disagreements in Congress.

Bryan Waller Procter.fact: His daughter, Adelaide Anne Procter, also became a popular poet, encouraged by Charles Dickens.

Fitz-Greene Halleck.fact: For years he worked as a private secretary to John Jacob Astor, then the richest man in America.

Charles Dickens.fact: As a boy of twelve he worked in a factory, sticking labels on pots of boot polish.

Ulysses S. Grant.fact: His real first name was Hiram; a mix-up at West Point turned him into Ulysses S. Grant.

Thomas Tusser.fact: His rhyming farming advice was so popular that it was reprinted many times in the 1500s and 1600s.

Francis Quarles.fact: His Emblems pairs short poems with pictures, and it was one of the best-selling books of its century.

John Bunyan.fact: Before becoming a writer he worked as a tinker, mending pots and pans just like his father.

John Dyer.fact: His long poem The Fleece is all about sheep, wool and the people who work with them.

John Home.fact: He later worked as private secretary to the Earl of Bute, who went on to become Prime Minister.

Duke of Wellington.fact: Wellington boots are named after him, because he had his boots made in a new, practical style.

Jane Taylor.fact: She wrote many poems for children with her sister Ann, in books such as Original Poems for Infant Minds.

Samuel Woodworth.fact: He trained as a printer in Boston and later published newspapers and magazines in New York.

Charles Wolfe.fact: He is remembered mainly for one poem, which was first printed without his name and became widely famous.

Charles Darwin.fact: Darwin spent five years sailing around the world as a naturalist aboard the ship HMS Beagle.

Bayard Taylor.fact: As a young man he toured Europe largely on foot, then wrote a bestseller about it called Views A-Foot.

Grover Cleveland.fact: Before becoming president, he served as mayor of Buffalo and then as governor of New York.

Quintilian.fact: He urged teachers to make learning fun for small children and to use praise rather than punishment.

Nicolas Boileau.fact: His poem The Art of Poetry set out rules for good writing that guided French poets for generations.

Michael Drayton.fact: His huge poem Poly-Olbion describes the landscape, rivers and history of England and Wales.

John Donne.fact: For the last ten years of his life he was Dean of St Paul's Cathedral in London.

Philip Massinger.fact: His comedy A New Way to Pay Old Debts stayed popular on the stage for more than 200 years.

Thomas Heywood.fact: He claimed to have helped write about 220 plays, though only a few dozen of them survive.

Francis Beaumont.fact: His comedy The Knight of the Burning Pestle has a grocer from the audience who keeps interrupting the play.

George Wither.fact: His poems were rediscovered two centuries later and warmly praised by the essayist Charles Lamb.

James Shirley.fact: When London's theatres were closed in the 1640s, he earned his living as a schoolmaster.

Sir William Davenant.fact: He helped create The Siege of Rhodes in 1656, often called the first English opera.

Thomas Otway.fact: His tragedy Venice Preserv'd was one of the most often performed plays in England for over a century.

Sir Richard Steele.fact: He wrote The Tatler under the made-up name Isaac Bickerstaff, borrowed from a joke by Jonathan Swift.

George Farquhar.fact: His comedy The Recruiting Officer was the first play ever staged in Australia, in 1789.

John Byrom.fact: Byrom coined the names "Tweedledum and Tweedledee" in a poem about two quarrelling musicians.

Matthew Green.fact: He spent his working life as a clerk at the Custom House in London, writing poems in his spare time.

Henry Fielding.fact: Fielding helped found the Bow Street Runners, often called London's first professional police force.

Sir William Blackstone.fact: He gave the first university lectures on English law, at Oxford, starting in 1753.

Thomas Warton.fact: He became Poet Laureate in 1785 and wrote the first full history of English poetry.

John Logan.fact: He gave popular public lectures on the history of the world in Edinburgh around 1780.

John Trumbull.fact: A brilliant child, he passed the entrance exam for Yale College at seven, though he started there later.

Walter Savage Landor.fact: Charles Dickens admired him so much that he named one of his sons Walter Landor Dickens.

Horace Smith.fact: Smith wrote a sonnet about Ozymandias in a friendly contest with his friend Percy Bysshe Shelley.

Allan Cunningham.fact: He began work as a stonemason's apprentice before becoming a writer in London.

Winthrop Mackworth Praed.fact: As a pupil at Eton he started a lively school magazine called The Etonian.

George Pope Morris.fact: He wrote the poem Woodman, Spare That Tree!, which became a popular song in the 1800s.

Mary Howitt.fact: She was one of the first people to translate Hans Christian Andersen's fairy tales into English.

Eliza Cook.fact: She ran her own weekly magazine, Eliza Cook's Journal, from 1849 to 1854.

Nathaniel Parker Willis.fact: He gave a young Edgar Allan Poe a job at his New York newspaper, the Evening Mirror.

Charles Kingsley.fact: He wrote Westward Ho!, and a seaside village in Devon was later named after the book.

Alexander Smith.fact: He worked as a designer of lace patterns in Glasgow before becoming famous for his poems.

Juvenal.fact: Very little is known about his life; most of what we know comes from hints in his own poems.

Alain-René Lesage.fact: He also wrote dozens of short comic plays for the lively fairground theatres of Paris.

Johann Wolfgang von Goethe.fact: He was also a keen scientist and wrote a book called Theory of Colours, published in 1810.

Washington Irving.fact: His pen name Diedrich Knickerbocker inspired the name of the New York Knicks basketball team.

George Washington.fact: Washington never lived in the White House, which was finished just after his time as president.

Abraham Lincoln.fact: Lincoln is the only US president to hold a patent, for a device to lift boats over shallow water.

Patrick Henry.fact: He became the first governor of Virginia after it declared independence from Britain in 1776.

Horace Walpole.fact: Walpole coined the word "serendipity" in a letter he wrote to a friend in 1754.

Tobias Smollett.fact: Before writing novels, he worked as a surgeon's mate on a Royal Navy ship.

Thomas Hobbes.fact: Still busy in old age, he translated all of Homer's Iliad and Odyssey into English verse in his eighties.

Thomas Carew.fact: He served at the court of King Charles I, where his job included serving dishes at the royal table.

John Quincy Adams.fact: After his presidency he went on to serve in the House of Representatives for 17 years.

Jean-Jacques Rousseau.fact: He was also a composer, and his short opera The Village Soothsayer was a hit in Paris in 1752.

Martial.fact: He was born in Bilbilis, in Hispania, in what is now Spain, and moved to Rome as a young man.

Edward Everett Hale.fact: His 1869 story The Brick Moon is one of the first stories about an artificial satellite.

Francis Bret Harte.fact: He edited the Overland Monthly magazine in San Francisco and was friends with Mark Twain.

Henry David Thoreau.fact: He worked in his family's pencil business and helped improve the way their pencils were made.

Jane Austen.fact: Her first novels were published without her name; Sense and Sensibility was signed only "By a Lady".

Mark Twain.fact: Before becoming a writer, he worked as a steamboat pilot on the Mississippi River.

Oscar Wilde.fact: He also wrote fairy tales for children, such as The Happy Prince and The Selfish Giant.

Emily Dickinson.fact: She was a keen gardener and, as a teenager, made an album of hundreds of pressed plants and flowers.

Ella Wheeler Wilcox.fact: She began publishing poems as a teenager while growing up on a farm in Wisconsin.

Robert Louis Stevenson.fact: He drew a treasure map with his stepson first, then wrote Treasure Island around it.

Lewis Carroll.fact: Lewis Carroll was a pen name; his real name was Charles Lutwidge Dodgson.

Jerome K. Jerome.fact: His comic book Three Men in a Boat includes a mischievous fox terrier named Montmorency.
